title: Supreme Court Seat Expansion via Ordinance: Constitutional Questions and Institutional Risks
description: Context: The Supreme Court of India is facing a significant constitutional debate after the President issued an Article 123 Ordinance raising the court’s sanctioned judicial strength from 34 to 38. About Supreme Court Seat Expansion via Ordinance: Constitutional Questions and Institutional Risks: The Calculated Risk: The Collegium’s Strategic Math The Supreme Court currently sits at 37 active judges. Legal experts reveal that the Collegium intentionally left the 38th seat vacant and carefully mapped out the appointments based on the judicial retirement calendar to transition the temporary judges into permanent seats: Key Conceptual and Institutional Challenges: Example: In D.C. Wadhwa vs State of Bihar (1986), the court ruled that governing through repromulgated ordinances is a fraud on the Constitution, a principle backed by the 2017 Krishna Kumar Singh judgment against parallel executive legislation. Example: Because the ruling political majority must pass the Bill to regularize their jobs, the court’s necessary detachment is compromised when that same Union Government appears before them as a primary litigant. Example: While past decisions like Gokaraju Rangaraju (1981) protect their rulings under the de facto doctrine, a lapse would leave a judge holding a post that the law no longer recognizes. Example: In the 2015 NJAC case, the court struck down a constitutional amendment to preserve its primary role in appointments, yet it has now left its bench strength dependent on executive goodwill. By matching its judicial appointments to the ticking clock of parliamentary sessions and upcoming retirements, the Supreme Court has taken a highly calculated institutional risk. While political numbers suggest the government will regularize the seats, the deeper issue is that the judiciary has staked its security of tenure on the goodwill of the political branch. True judicial independence requires more than just the authority to check executive power—it relies on an unyielding institutional instinct to protect its own separation from it. “Judicial independence is sustained not only through constitutional safeguards but also through institutional conventions.” Examine the constitutional mechanisms ensuring judicial independence in India. Analyse emerging challenges to judicial autonomy. (10 M)

title: Beyond the Prison Walls: A Song of Second Chances
description: Anecdote: One Sunday afternoon, listeners tuning into Akashvani Bhadravathi expected familiar melodies. Instead, they heard voices carrying a deeper resonance—not of professional singers, but of inmates from the Central Prison in Shivamogga. Through a unique programme titled Jailu Hakkigala Gaanasudhe (Melodies of the Caged Birds), men once defined by their crimes found a new identity as artists, storytellers, and human beings seeking redemption. Among them was Thimmappa, a former teacher. He chose to sing Manavaredeyali, a song whose poignant message reminds us that the very hands capable of violence are also capable of compassion. His choice was more than a musical performance; it was a quiet confession of human complexity and the possibility of transformation. Another inmate, Dadapeer, sang Amma Ninna Yedeyaladalli, a song dedicated to a mother’s unconditional love. As he recalled his mother’s struggles and her death shortly after his imprisonment, the song transcended entertainment and became a moving expression of remorse, loss, and longing. In that moment, listeners heard not a prisoner, but a son. The programme demonstrated a profound truth: while prisons may confine bodies, they need not imprison the human spirit. Through music, literature, theatre, and poetry, inmates are reminded that they remain capable of creativity, reflection, and moral growth. The initiative reflects a progressive philosophy of criminal justice. Punishment alone may deter wrongdoing, but rehabilitation seeks something greater—the restoration of human dignity and reintegration into society. By giving inmates a platform, society communicates that mistakes need not become permanent identities. The story is a powerful reminder that redemption often begins when individuals are seen not merely as offenders but as persons with talents, emotions, and the capacity to change. Like rough stones polished by time, opportunities for expression can reveal virtues hidden beneath past mistakes. Ultimately, Jailu Hakkigala Gaanasudhe is not merely a radio programme. It is a testament to the belief that every individual deserves a second chance, and that compassion, when combined with accountability, can transform lives more effectively than punishment alone.
